The stipend landed on the 1st at 10:14 a.m. Tanmay saw the bank message during a lab class in Pune and grinned. By evening he had bought new earphones, treated three friends to biryani, and ordered the hoodie he had been eyeing for weeks.
On the 19th his wallet held forty rupees. He ate the plain mess food twice a day and skipped the film outing Bidisha was organising. His mother, Lakshmi, called; he said everything was fine.
That night he opened his notes and typed: "Next month: 3,000 into savings on day one. No exceptions."
On the 1st, the message came at 10:09. By noon he was at the electronics shop near college, "just looking".

qa.q: How much money did Tanmay have on the 19th?
qa.a: On the 19th his wallet held forty rupees.

qa.q: Why did Tanmay feel sure that next month would be different?
qa.a: Tanmay felt hopeful and determined once he had typed the plan, as if the problem were already solved while he was broke and missing the outing.

qa.q: What choice on the 1st could stop Tanmay's loop?
qa.a: He could move the savings the moment the message arrives, before class ends, so there is no money left to spend 'just looking' at the shop.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi feel if she learned the truth behind 'everything was fine'?
qa.a: She might be worried that her son was eating little and hiding it, and wish he had told her so they could plan together.

grounding: Shows a student who spends his stipend right away and promises a careful next month that repeats the same pattern.

"Relax, didi. The hostel fee is paid."
"And the rest? Mummy sent you train fare because you said you were broke."
Their mother, Sarika, stopped rolling rotis. "Broke on the fifteenth again?"
"I needed the shoes. And the trip was a one-time thing."
"Last month it was the one-time concert," Lavanya said.
"I know, I know." Nikhil rubbed his face. "Next month I'm putting half into savings the day it comes. Promise."
"You said that in March."
"This time I mean it. I really want the laptop by December."
Sarika slid a roti onto his plate. "Meaning it isn't the hard part, beta."

passage:
I'm Saurabh, final-year engineering, and here's my confession about the fellowship money. Eight thousand rupees every month. Each time it arrives I feel rich for about four days: a trek with the club, a new keyboard, dinners I insist on paying for.
Even while tapping "pay", I know that in three weeks I'll want that money for exam fees and the bus home. I tell myself next month will be the disciplined one.
Sonali, who shares my lab bench, keeps a little table of her spending in a notebook. I used to tease her about it, and she calls me Mr Four Days. Last month, on the 22nd, I borrowed five hundred from her. Her table suddenly didn't look so funny.
The next stipend came. I'd planned to save half. I saved nothing. Again.

qa.q: How much did Saurabh borrow from Sonali, and when?
qa.a: He borrowed five hundred from Sonali on the 22nd.

qa.q: How does Saurabh feel about his spending when he looks back?
qa.a: He feels sheepish and frustrated with himself; he knew while paying that he would need the money, and ends with 'Again'. 😔

qa.q: What could Saurabh copy from Sonali to break the pattern?
qa.a: He could keep his own small table and set aside the exam-fee and bus money on the first day, so the four rich days only use what is left.

qa.q: How might Sonali see Saurabh after lending him money?
qa.a: Sonali may feel quietly proved right about the notebook, and also wonder whether the next stipend will bring the same request.

grounding: Shows a student who spends a monthly stipend quickly, fully aware he will want it later, and repeats this every month.

Student mentor's note, 6 March (Disha, faculty mentor)
Anand, 20, came to see me today asking for an advance on next month's research stipend. This is the third month in a row.
The stipend arrives on the 1st. By his own account, on the 1st he bought new shoes, on the 2nd he paid for a friend's birthday dinner, and by the 5th he had ordered a phone case and concert tickets. He knew his mess fees were due on the 10th.
He said, "Every month I tell myself, next month I'll be disciplined. And then the money comes and next month feels far away." He looked embarrassed and tired.
I did not lecture. I asked him to describe the 10th of next month in detail: where he'll be, what he'll need. He went quiet.
Next: I've referred him to the student welfare office's money-planning session and will check in on the 2nd.

qa.q: When does Anand's stipend arrive?
qa.a: The stipend arrives on the 1st.

qa.q: How does Anand feel about his spending, and what shows it?
qa.a: Anand feels embarrassed and tired, admitting that each month he promises to be disciplined, but when the money comes next month feels far away.

qa.q: Which step by Disha could help Anand, and why?
qa.a: Asking him to picture the 10th in detail makes his future needs feel real at the moment of choosing, and the welfare office session gives him practical support.

qa.q: How might Disha feel hearing Anand ask for an advance for the third month?
qa.a: Disha seems concerned but patient, choosing not to lecture and instead asking Anand to picture the 10th and referring him to the money-planning session.

grounding: It shows a student spending his stipend at once, knowing he will need it later, and promising to be disciplined next month before repeating the choice.

3 August, night
Scholarship money came this morning. Six thousand. By lunch I'd bought the cricket bat I've wanted since June. Then Jasleen said the whole gang was going for momos and a film, and I paid for tickets because I was "rich".
Rajni didi called at nine. "Harshit, keep some for the lab manual and the bus pass, you know you'll need it by the 20th." I said, "Yes, didi, I'm your sensible little brother now." I meant it.
Checked the account after she hung up. One thousand four hundred left.
The weird part is, last month I wrote in this same diary: "Next month, save first." I remember writing it. It felt so easy last month.
Next month. Seriously. September me will be different.
Harshit

qa.q: How does Harshit feel about the money, and how does that change?
qa.a: Harshit feels "rich" and happy spending on the bat, momos and the film, then shocked to see only one thousand four hundred left, though he still hopes September will be different.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could Harshit try when the money comes next time?
qa.a: He spent before setting anything aside; next time he could keep the lab manual and bus pass money apart first, perhaps with Rajni didi's help, before any treats.

qa.q: How might Rajni didi feel if she saw the account after the call?
qa.a: Rajni didi would likely feel worried and a little frustrated, since Harshit promised to be sensible just minutes before checking the balance.

passage:
1 October
Stipend came today. Eight thousand. This month I was going to keep half aside for the trip in December; I promised myself last month. By 9 p.m.: new earphones, dinner with Tanvir at the rooftop place, a hoodie that was on sale (it WAS on sale). Nothing left for the trip pot. Again.
Tanvir asked how I always run out by the tenth. I said I'm starting properly next month, and I meant it. Then I scrolled back in this diary. 1 September: "Starting properly next month." 1 August: same.
It's weird. In August, December felt real. Today, the earphones felt more real. I think the problem is that 'next month' is always somebody else.
Tushar

qa.a: Tanvir notices that Tushar always runs out by the tenth, and asks about it with curiosity rather than judgement.

passage: On the day the scholarship money reached the small college in Namchi, the whole hostel went to town. Pema had planned it carefully the night before: keep most of it for the books and the bus pass, spend a little. But the market was bright with Losar decorations, her friends were laughing, there was a new jacket in a shop window, and hot momos for everyone, her treat. By evening the envelope was thin. Hafsa, her roommate, watched her count it on the bed. "The books?" "Next month," Pema said. "Next month I'll be good." Hafsa said nothing, but Pema remembered saying exactly that in the same room, on the same bed, three months ago. She pushed the jacket bag under the bed and felt her stomach turn.

passage: On the first of each month, Emeka's stipend landed in his account at the university in Stockholm. By the fifth, it was mostly gone: a new jacket, dinners out, a concert ticket, a speaker. The twentieth feels like someone else's problem." Anders suggested he talk to the student finance adviser on campus about ways to set some aside before he saw it. Emeka went the next week, a bit embarrassed. He came back with a plan he'd chosen himself.

Dear Parul didi,
You asked about my stipend, so here's the honest answer: it's gone again, and it's only the ninth.
I know I promised last month. I was going to put some aside the moment it came. But on the first, there was a sale on shoes I actually needed, and then my friends were going for dinner, and then a festival ticket. Each thing felt small and right. The end of the month felt so far away.
And now I'm eating instant noodles and asking you for help, again.
I think the problem is I always plan to be careful "next month." Next-month Chinmay is a very good person. This-month Chinmay is not.
Could we talk on Sunday? You're good at this. Maybe you can help me set something up before the first comes.
Your brother,
Chinmay

1 August. Pema's research stipend hit the account. By evening: a new jacket, a weekend trip with the lab group, momos for everyone. "From September I'll save half," Pema told Sangeeta at dinner, and meant it.
1 September. The stipend landed again. There was a sale on headphones. Pema bought them, and then the lab group planned a birthday dinner. "October," Pema said. "Definitely October."
20 September. Rent was due, and Pema's account showed three hundred rupees. Sangeeta, a senior in the lab, sat Pema down with two cups of tea, not to scold but to plan. "Every month you promise the following month, and that month is always a different you. Why not ask the bank today how to move some of it on the first, before you see it?"
Pema stared at the tea, then took out a phone and opened the bank's help page.

Imran beta, you've come to ask for an advance again? Sit, have tea. I'm Rekha Aunty, I've run this hostel mess for thirty-five years, and let me tell you about a boy who ate here long ago. Sunil. Clever boy, engineering, like you.
Every month his scholarship came, and in three days it was gone: films, new shirts, samosas for everyone. Every month he told me, "Aunty, next month I'll save." And every month, the same.
Then in his final year his father fell sick, and Sunil had no money for the train home. He sat on that bench and cried. I lent him the fare.
After that he did one thing. The day the scholarship came, before buying anything, he asked the bank to move part of it into a deposit he couldn't easily touch.
He runs a company now. He still sends me a sari every Diwali.

qa.q: What did Sunil buy for everyone?
qa.a: Sunil bought samosas for everyone.

qa.q: Why did Sunil keep spending the scholarship within three days?
qa.a: Sunil felt happy and generous in the moment, and saving felt like a job for a later self who never arrived.

qa.q: Which choice in the story changed Sunil's pattern, and why?
qa.a: Asking the bank to move part of the scholarship into a deposit on the day it came, so the choice was made before temptation.

qa.q: How might Sunil have felt on the bench in his final year?
qa.a: Sunil was likely frightened and ashamed, unable to go home to a sick father after spending the money.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a student who spent his scholarship at once each month and kept promising to save next month.
